answer: A registry can make sybil identities costly by fusing each agent's signing key into a sealed chip. Enrollment requires the chip to answer a fresh challenge, and enrollments per die are capped, so an attacker needs one device per identity: cost goes linear rather than flat. Since the key cannot be copied out, a farm of hollow identities fails attestation, and revoking a die kills every identity it spawned, so a comet of registrations across many addresses collapses to the dies owned. Each die also reports a stable pigment, a spectral signature sampled at boot, so duplicates surface at once.
